rv.q: And yet I say this only to preface a thousand words about how instantly transporting and delightful the musical is.
Even when it veers toward corny sentimentality, the show’s thematic focus on the resilience and hopefulness of youth exerts a persuasive pull.
If there's a criticism to be made, it's that the sweet book, lovable characters, and universal themes are all too familiar.
It’s the show that surrounds it that still needs fine tuning.

Enjoyable, admirable and starring a superabundance of talented actor-musicians, many of them still in their teens, Sing Street is nevertheless so slim it seems to disappear before the last note has sounded.
There’s not a clunker among them—even the synth-heavy purposely simplistic “The Riddle of the Model” is a toe-tapper—but you’ll be singing the defiant anthem “Drive It Like You Stole It” for days.

And while Sing Street is a lot of fun when the company lets loose with adolescent fury, it's those personal connections and softer moments that bring out its whole-hearted warmth and uplifting optimism.
Overflowing with charm and heart, Sing Street is about the thrill of first love and the power of music.
Sing Street is still a charmingly offbeat foray down memory lane that captures the restless mood of an economically depressed but culturally rich period in recent Irish history.

By stripping the story of local color—even the projections show little but an anonymous seascape—the creative team does ill by Sing Street. Take away the Irish accents, the 1980’s songs and a quick reference to The Famine, and this story of alienated teens could have taken place in Boise, Idaho, or Buenos Aires, Argentina.
Sing Street, despite some weaknesses, makes an adequately entertaining evening; but I expect once is enough.
But “Sing Street” the stage musical is likely to disappoint anybody who has seen “Sing Street” the movie (which is currently available for viewing online, through IMDB TV, for free.)
Sing Street wants to be the next Once, but lightning has not struck twice.
Sing Street wants you to believe in the magic of music, but it never really sings.
Most of what’s fresh and appealing in the film (which is cheerfully formulaic) has been lost in a leaden theatrical frame that saps milieu, character and music-making of any tension or charm.
It is a feel-good musical that is neither mawkish nor incredible and strips away extravagance to embellish the fortitude of ordinary people.

While director Rebecca Taichman’s production offers moments of transcendence, particularly in the often-luminous second act, the show needs needs some additional polish on its hero’s defiantly brown shoes.
But it felt like something was missing.

cn.t: A charming but slight adaptation that lacks the magic of its predecessor "Once." The talented young cast and nostalgic '80s pastiche songs impress, but critics find the show disappointingly thin and unfulfilled.
